
Three readings of @fig-fourth-down.

**The habit came first, the good team second.** Detroit's neutral go rate was `{python} S["det_gr2020"]` in 2020,
below the league. In Campbell's first season it was `{python} S["det_gr2021"]`, `{python} S["det_gr_rk2021"]` in
the league, for a team that won three games: the underdog logic from the start of this chapter. (Detroit led the
league in raw attempts that year; by this rate, which strips out desperate situations, it was a whisker behind
the leader's `{python} S["gr21_top"]`.) Then it *stayed*
near a third of neutral fourth downs, first in the league in 2022, 2023 and 2024
(`{python} S["det_gr2024"]` in 2024, against a league average of `{python} S["lg_gr2024"]`), after Detroit had
become a favourite. That is the more interesting decision, because the variance argument no longer applies. A
favourite going for it is betting on the expected-points case alone, and on its own offense.

**It paid, by a rough yardstick, though mostly in one season.** Detroit converted
`{python} S["det_conv"]` of its attempts in 2021–2025 (the league converted `{python} S["lg_conv"]`). Converting is
the wrong test, though, as [10-04](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) argued: what
matters is the attempt compared with the kick it replaced. So compare each of Detroit's `{python} S["det_n_q3"]`
first-three-quarter attempts with what the league's punts and field goals produced from the same spots. The
attempts come out about `{python} S["det_gain"]` points ahead over five seasons, `{python} S["gain_rk"]` in the
league over the period. That total is lumpy: about `{python} S["gain24"]` came in 2024 alone, and the other four
seasons averaged about `{python} S["gain_other"]`.

The total is a net figure, and the bad tail is inside it. The conversions gained about `{python} S["det_win_pts"]`
points against kicking; the `{python} S["det_fail_n"]` failures gave back about `{python} S["det_fail_pts"]`.
Each failure hands the opponent a short field, and the ones that come late in close games are the ones fans
remember. The yardstick is also crude. Teams go for it when they like their chances, so the attempts are a
selected sample, and that same selection is why the *league average* go in @fig-fourth-down looks worth
`{python} S["lg_per"]` points over kicking: the average go looks good partly because teams only go when it looks
good. A proper answer needs a win-probability model of each decision, which is built in
[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd). But
the direction for Detroit is not in doubt.

**The more you go, the less each go is worth.** Detroit's value *per attempt* (`{python} S["det_per"]` points) was
only a little above the league's (`{python} S["lg_per"]`), and well below the Eagles (`{python} S["per_PHI"]`) and
the Chiefs (`{python} S["per_KC"]`). The reason shows up inside Detroit's own attempts. The first fourth downs a
coach adds are the obvious ones, fourth-and-1 or 2 near midfield; the next ones are closer calls, and
`{python} S["det_long"]` of Detroit's attempts came with four or more yards to go, against `{python} S["lg_long"]`
for the league. Detroit's attempts with one to three yards to go were worth `{python} S["det_short_per"]` points
each against kicking; its attempts with four or more were worth `{python} S["det_long_per"]`. That is diminishing
returns: each extra, longer attempt is still slightly positive on average, but adds far less than the short ones,
and it fails more often. (The right panel of @fig-fourth-down can't show this on its own: across teams, attempts
and value per attempt are nearly uncorrelated, `{python} S["n_per_corr"]`, because teams differ in far more than
aggressiveness.)

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Campbell is a gambler." A gambler takes bets with negative expected value for the thrill. Campbell's fourth-down
record is a long series of bets with *positive* expected value, some of which lost, a few of them in playoff
games. The fair criticism is narrower: in a handful of late, high-leverage spots (the 2023 NFC Championship Game,
covered in [10-04](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd), is the famous one), the models themselves called the decision close, and a coach with a strong kicker might reasonably
have kicked. Judge the habit by the whole record, and the close calls by the odds before the snap.
:::

The habit extended past the field. Detroit's front office took its aggressive streak to the league's rule-making
meetings: a Lions proposal produced the 2024 rule that gives a coach a third challenge when *either* of his first
two succeeds (it had required both),[^challenge] and in 2025 the Lions proposed letting wild-card teams with better
records be seeded above division winners, a proposal withdrawn before a vote.[^seeding] A team that thinks in
expected value tends to notice where the rules leave value on the table.

## How opponents responded

Defenses had answers, and they were the standard ones for this kind of offense. None of them is specific to
Detroit's opponents in any one game; they are what defensive coaches teach against under-center play-action, jumbo
and heavy motion:

- **Keep the backside end home.** On a run fake away from him, the end on the boot side doesn't chase; he stays to
  meet the bootlegging quarterback. That is the reason the leak in @fig-jumbo has to come out on time.
- **Give the reported lineman an owner.** A linebacker or the walked-down safety takes #70 if he releases, so the
  leak is covered and the bait still has to beat the defenders underneath.
- **Play single-high and accept the risk.** Two deep safeties stop the play-action shots but leave a light box
  for the run game, so many defenses chose the other trade: a safety down, eight in the box, and a deep shot
  given up now and then. Detroit saw two-high coverage on `{python} S["two_det24"]` of its 2024 dropbacks against a
  league average of `{python} S["two_lg24"]` (`{python} S["two_det24_rk"]` of 32 teams, where 1st means the most
  two-high), so slightly more single-high than most. The gap is small, so read it as a lean, not a strategy.
- **Simplify against motion.** Instead of rotating with every shift and motion, a defense can "lock" its
  coverage (nobody travels, nobody rotates) and play the call it started with, accepting a worse match-up in
  exchange for no busts.

None of these took the offense away: it ranked `{python} S["det_epa_rk2022"]`, `{python} S["det_epa_rk2023"]` and
`{python} S["det_epa_rk2024"]` in EPA per play from 2022 to 2024.
The worst day came in January 2025, in the divisional round against Washington. Detroit, the
`{python} S["rec_DET_2024"]` top seed, lost 45–31 after turning the ball over five times: four interceptions, one
of them returned for a touchdown, and a lost fumble. Two of the trick plays in the table above came in that game.
It wasn't a scheme answer so much as the bad tail of a high-variance team arriving on the worst day, against a
Detroit defense that had been gutted by injuries since October: Aidan Hutchinson broke his leg in the 47–9 win at
Dallas, and by December the injured defenders also included Alim McNeill, Alex Anzalone and Carlton
Davis.[^injuries]

The league's response was the more durable one, and it came in two forms. The first was imitation, though the
Lions were one influence among several (by 2025 the Rams took more snaps from under center than anyone): league-wide, the
share of plays from under center went from about 27% in 2023 to about 34% in 2025, heavy personnel climbed to a
decade high, and the neutral fourth-down go rate kept rising.[^trend] The second was the coaching market. Within
three days in January 2025, the Lions lost both coordinators to head-coaching jobs: Johnson to the Chicago Bears,
a division rival, and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn to the New York Jets.[^depart] That is the usual price of
success for a staff, and it set up what economists call a *natural experiment*: nobody designed it, but the same
ideas now had one coach removed and two teams to compare. The rest of this chapter runs that comparison.

## After Johnson: Detroit in 2025 and 2026

Campbell hired John Morton, a veteran assistant, as offensive coordinator and play-caller, and Kelvin Sheppard
replaced Glenn as defensive coordinator. After a loss to Minnesota in Week 9, Campbell took the play sheet himself,
starting with a 44–22 win over Washington.[^morton] The Lions finished `{python} S["rec_DET_2025"]` and missed the
playoffs. The offense was still good, `{python} S["det_epa_rk2025"]` in EPA per play, with the same quarterback,
receivers and running backs, but no longer great, and it looked more like everyone else's (though still
well above the league's habits): under center
`{python} S["uc_DET_2025"]` of the time (from `{python} S["uc_DET_2024"]`), play-action on `{python} S["pa_DET_2025"]`
of dropbacks (from `{python} S["pa_DET_2024"]`). [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
compares the offense under Morton and under Campbell in detail. After the season Morton was fired, and the Lions
hired Drew Petzing, previously the Cardinals' coordinator, as their third offensive coordinator in three years;
Sheppard stayed on defense.[^petzing]

The data in this chapter stop at the end of 2025, and the 2026 season is only weeks old as this is written, so
it is too early to say what Petzing's offense is. The test is easy to run yourself as the season goes on: if
Detroit's under-center and play-action rates in @fig-transfer climb back toward their 2024 levels, the habits
belonged to the building; if they stay near the league average, they left with Johnson.

## What transferred to Chicago

The Bears Johnson inherited were a classic Detroit-2021 problem: `{python} S["rec_CHI_2024"]` in 2024, an offense
`{python} S["chi_epa_rk2024"]` in EPA per play, and a rookie quarterback, Caleb Williams, sacked
`{python} S["chi_sk24"]` times. In 2025 they went `{python} S["rec_CHI_2025"]`, won the NFC North, beat Green Bay
31–27 in the wild-card round (the franchise's first playoff win since the 2010 season) and lost to the Rams 20–17 in overtime in the divisional round.[^bears25] The offense
jumped to `{python} S["chi_epa_rk2025"]` in EPA per play; Williams was sacked `{python} S["chi_sk25"]` times, and his
EPA per dropback rose from `{python} S["cw24_epa"]` to `{python} S["cw25_epa"]`.

How much of that is Johnson? @fig-transfer compares the two teams' fingerprints before and after he moved.

```{python}
#| label: fig-transfer
#| fig-cap: "What moved with Ben Johnson. Each arrow runs from a 2024 value to the 2025 value, for the Lions, the Bears and the league as a whole (grey), so you can see how much of a team's change was just the league moving. Under center, play-action and trick plays jumped in Chicago in Johnson's first season, to near the top of the league, and fell back in Detroit without him. Motion rose in Chicago by about twice the league's rise, but not to the top. Reported linemen rose in Chicago but only to about the league's new, higher level: that habit moved least. The fourth-down habit belonged to the other coach: Detroit stayed far more aggressive than the league under Campbell, while Chicago's go rate rose about as much as the league's did. Play-action is a share of dropbacks; under center and motion are shares of runs and passes; reported linemen and trick plays are per 100 runs and passes (a report from the official play-by-play; FTN's trick-play flag); the go rate uses neutral fourth downs as in the previous figure. FTN doesn't chart shifts, so the shift habit can't be measured this way. Sources: FTN charting via nflverse; nflverse play-by-play."
METRICS = [("Under center (% of plays)", HAB["uc"] * 100, HABL["uc"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Play-action (% of dropbacks)", HAB["pa"] * 100, HABL["pa"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Motion (% of plays)", HAB["mo"] * 100, HABL["mo"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Reported linemen (per 100 plays)", HAB["rep"], HABL["rep"], "{:.1f}"),
           ("Trick plays (per 100 plays)", HAB["tr"], HABL["tr"], "{:.1f}"),
           ("Neutral 4th-down go rate (%)", GR.loc[2022:] * 100, LGR.loc[2022:] * 100, "{:.0f}%")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.6))
for ax, (title, tab, lg, fmt) in zip(axes.flat, METRICS):
    rows = [("Lions", LIONS, tab.loc[[2024, 2025], "DET"].values),
            ("Bears", BEARS, tab.loc[[2024, 2025], "CHI"].values),
            ("League", style.MUTED, lg.loc[[2024, 2025]].values)]
    hi = max(max(v) for _, _, v in rows)
    for i, (team, col, v) in enumerate(rows):
        y = 2 - i
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((v[0], y), (v[1], y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=col, lw=1.9,
                                     shrinkA=3, shrinkB=1))
        ax.plot([v[0]], [y], marker="o", ms=3.8, color=col, mfc="white", mew=1.3)
        up = v[0] < v[1]
        ax.text(v[0] + (-1 if up else 1) * 0.03 * hi, y + 0.33, fmt.format(v[0]), fontsize=6.3,
                ha="right" if up else "left", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
        ax.text(v[1] + (1 if up else -1) * 0.03 * hi, y + 0.33, fmt.format(v[1]), fontsize=6.3,
                ha="left" if up else "right", va="center", color=style.INK if team == "League" else col,
                fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_yticks([2, 1, 0], ["Lions", "Bears", "League"], fontsize=7.2)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 2.75)
    ax.set_xlim(0, hi * 1.3)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.6)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=style.INK_2, marker="o", mfc="white", lw=1.6, label="2024 → 2025")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=1, fontsize=7, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.9, w_pad=1.4, rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

The picture is unusually clean for football data, at least for the three most visible habits. In one offseason,
Chicago went from `{python} S["uc_CHI_2024_rk"]` to `{python} S["uc_CHI_2025_rk"]` in under-center rate
(`{python} S["uc_CHI_2024"]` to `{python} S["uc_CHI_2025"]`), from `{python} S["pa_CHI_2024_rk"]` to
`{python} S["pa_CHI_2025_rk"]` in play-action share (`{python} S["pa_CHI_2024"]` to `{python} S["pa_CHI_2025"]`),
and from `{python} S["tr_CHI_2024_rk"]` to `{python} S["tr_CHI_2025_rk"]` in trick-play rate. Detroit's numbers
moved the other way. Those habits were the play-caller's, and they travelled with him.

The other two habits moved less. Chicago's motion rate rose from `{python} S["mo_CHI_2024v"]` to
`{python} S["mo_CHI_2025v"]` of plays (`{python} S["mo_CHI_2025_rk"]` in the league), about twice the league's
rise, but not to the top. Reported linemen rose from `{python} S["rep_CHI_2024v"]` to `{python} S["rep_CHI_2025v"]`
per 100 plays, in a year when the whole league jumped from `{python} S["rep_lg_2024v"]` to
`{python} S["rep_lg_2025v"]`, so Chicago ended up slightly *below* the league average. A habit that depends on
personnel (a sixth lineman Johnson trusts as a blocker and as a decoy) takes longer to install than one that
depends on the play sheet. Shifts can't be measured from FTN's public charting at all.

The fourth-down habit didn't travel the same way. Detroit's neutral go rate fell from `{python} S["det_gr2024"]` to
`{python} S["det_gr2025"]` but stayed `{python} S["det_gr_rk2025"]` in the league under Campbell; Chicago's rose from
`{python} S["chi_gr24"]` to `{python} S["chi_gr25"]`, in a season when the whole league rose. Aggression on fourth
down had been the head coach's.

What the fingerprint can't tell you is how much of Chicago's improvement came from the scheme. The Bears also rebuilt
the middle of their offensive line before 2025, trading for guards Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson (a Lions starter in
Johnson's first two seasons as coordinator) and signing center Drew Dalman,[^bearsol] and Williams was in his second
season, when most young quarterbacks improve. The sack total falling from `{python} S["chi_sk24"]` to
`{python} S["chi_sk25"]` belongs to all three. In short: the play-caller's signature habits transferred at once,
the personnel-dependent ones partly; the *results* transferred substantially, with help.

## What survives

The Johnson-Campbell Lions lasted four seasons as a unit, from 2021 to 2024, and they leave a few ideas that have
outlasted the staff.

- **Under center is a disguise, not a throwback.** The Lions, with the Rams, showed that a modern passing
  offense can take a large share of its snaps from under center at no cost, and throw unusually well off the run
  fake, because the fake and the run look the same. The league followed.
- **Personnel is a message you can lie with.** A reported lineman, a third tight end, a jumbo set: each tells the
  defense something, and an offense can choose whether to deliver on it.
- **Make the defense answer twice.** Shifts layered with motion turn a single snap into two or three communication
  tests. Most defenses pass most of them; the offense only needs the occasional failure.
- **Trick plays are part of the system.** Built on the defense's habits and the offense's own self-scout, they are
  constraint plays with a sense of humour, and their cost is visible on the bad days.
- **Fourth-down aggression became normal, and its edge got smaller.** When one team goes for it a third of the time,
  it's a strategy; when the league catches up, the remaining edge is in choosing *which* fourth downs, which is a
  harder skill to see from the stands.
- **A rebuild can choose variance.** A bad team that plays to the expected-value math and accepts the ugly
  failures can turn into a good team that keeps doing it, which is what Detroit did.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the trick detector"}
Pick a Lions or Bears game (or any team that runs a lot from under center) and flag every snap with something
unusual in it.

- **Before the snap, listen.** "Number 70 is reporting as eligible": note the down and distance. Then watch the
  safeties, not the lineman. If they creep down, expect the run fake and a throw behind them.
- **Count the movements.** One mark for a shift, one for a motion. Snaps with two or more marks are the ones where
  the defense has to communicate twice; look for a defender still pointing or moving at the snap.
- **Find the odd alignment.** A quarterback split wide, a running back alone in the backfield taking a direct snap,
  a receiver stacked right behind another one a yard off the line, a tackle at the end of the line. Write down
  what the defense did about it.
- **After the snap: who caught the first ball?** On a short catch near the sideline, keep your eyes on the player
  *behind* the catcher. If someone is trailing at full speed, the hook-and-lateral is on.
- **On fourth down, guess first.** Before the offense decides, say go, kick or punt using the rules of thumb from
  10-04. Then compare with what the coach did, and note whether he was more or less aggressive than you.
- **At the end of the game,** count your flags and how many of them gained yards. You have just charted a team's
  disguise rate, the raw material for a [tendency report](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-report).
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** Second-and-5 at your own 35, first quarter. The offense comes out in @fig-predict-1: six offensive
linemen, number 70 has reported eligible and stands at the right end of the line, the quarterback is under center
and the defense has walked a safety down, with only one deep safety left. You have seen this offense run from this
look three times already today. What is the most likely play, and where is the ball going?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: jumbo with a reported tackle (#70), second-and-5. The strong safety (ringed) has come down to about six yards deep, just outside #70, making eight defenders in the box; one deep safety remains."
off, dfn = jumbo_look()
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.2, w=5.6) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=5, title="Drill 1: number 70 has reported eligible")
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.highlight("T70")
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-9.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (10.2, 9.8), (6.2, 5.6), "safety walked down:\neight in the box")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.6, 8.4), (-0.7, 4.8), "#70 reported eligible")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (15.0, 7.4), (13.5, -0.5), "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A play-action pass behind the safety, most likely to a receiver crossing into the space he left.** Everything
in the picture says run: second-and-5 (a run-friendly down), six linemen, a quarterback under center, and you've
seen runs from it. The defense agrees, which is why the safety is down. That is the bait half of @fig-jumbo. With
eight defenders committed to the run and one deep safety in the middle, the space behind the linebackers and
outside the deep safety is open for a moment after the run fake.

Why not the leak to #70, the player the question is about? Look where the safety walked down: just outside #70.
A lineman slipping into the flat would run straight into him. The leak is the backup, and it's best when the
walked-down safety is on the *other* side and the linebackers flow hard away from #70. A plain run is still
possible, but the offense has spent three snaps teaching this defense to bring the safety down. Detroit cashed
exactly this kind of setup in Week 18 of 2023: on second-and-5 with Dan Skipper reported eligible, Goff faked the
run and hit St. Brown for a 70-yard touchdown (the play is in
[Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Fourth-and-4 at the opponent's 35, second quarter, score tied. @fig-predict-2 shows the field. Your
kicker makes about two-thirds of his kicks from 50 to 54 yards. What would the 2022–2024 Lions have done, what
would a typical NFL team have done, and if Detroit goes for it, what will the offense look like?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: fourth-and-4 at the opponent's 35 (offense moving left to right). A field goal from here is about a 53-yard kick: 35 yards to the goal line, 10 more to the goalposts at the back of the end zone, and about 8 for the snap and hold. A punt would net perhaps 20 to 25 yards."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.6))
LOS, Y0 = 110 - 35, 26.65
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=LOS, window=(-24, 46), to_go=4, numbers=False, hashes=True,
            lateral=(13.0, 40.3))
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((LOS, Y0), 1.6, 1.0, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))
for x, lab in [(60, "50"), (70, "40"), (80, "30"), (90, "20"), (100, "10"), (110, "G")]:
    ax.text(x, 15.0, lab, fontsize=8, ha="center", va="center", color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.TURF, ec="none"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(120, 35.2), xytext=(LOS - 8, 35.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
ax.text((LOS - 8 + 120) / 2, 37.6, "field goal: about a 53-yard kick (holder ~8 yards back; posts at the end line)",
        fontsize=7.0, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(LOS + 4, 21.0), xytext=(LOS, 21.0),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4))
ax.text(LOS + 5.0, 21.0, "4 yards for a first down", fontsize=7.2, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(LOS - 1.6, 28.6, "fourth-and-4,\nball on the\nopponent's 35", fontsize=7.0, ha="right", va="center",
        color=style.INK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(115, 24.0, "end\nzone", fontsize=7.4, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Detroit goes for it; most teams don't; and the play will be a shotgun pass.** This is the "go zone" from
[10-04](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd): the opponent's 30 to 40, too far for a
comfortable field goal (a 53-yarder at two-thirds or less) and too close for a punt to gain much, so the models
usually say go even on fourth-and-4 or 5. Teams mostly ignore that. On fourth-and-3 to 5 between the opponent's 30
and 40 in the first three quarters of 2022–2024, the league went for it `{python} S["lg_d45"]` of the time and
Detroit `{python} S["det_d45"]` (a small sample, `{python} S["det_d45_n"]` snaps). This is exactly where Campbell's
habit differed from everyone else's: not on fourth-and-1, where most teams now go, but on the medium-yardage
calls the models like and the sidelines still fear.

The play is the surprise. You might expect the under-center, play-action identity, and on fourth-and-1 or 2 you'd
be partly right: Detroit was under center on `{python} S["det_4s_uc"]` of those attempts (league
`{python} S["lg_4s_uc"]`) and used play-action on `{python} S["det_4s_pa"]` (league `{python} S["lg_4s_pa"]`). But
on fourth-and-3 to 5, Detroit was in the shotgun on all `{python} S["det_4m_n"]` of its attempts in 2022–2024,
and `{python} S["det_4m_db"]` were dropbacks, just like the league. When the down and distance tell the defense
"pass", there is nothing left to disguise, and even this offense lines up to throw. The menu isn't one play.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** Second-and-goal from the 3. The offense lines up in @fig-predict-3: the running back is alone in the
shotgun spot, the quarterback is split out in the left slot, and there are two tight ends to the right, one on the
line and one on the wing, with a receiver outside them. What is the default play, what is the trick, and whom should the defense not forget?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: a direct snap to the running back (R) at the 3-yard line, with the quarterback (Q) split out in the left slot and two tight ends (Y at the end of the line, U on the wing) to the right. X is on the line at the left end; Z is a yard off the line, outside U. Illustrative alignment."
off = line5() + [O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 0.0, "R"), O("QB", "QB", -1.5, -8.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -1.6, 6.4, "U"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.5, "Z")]
# seven on the line: X, the five linemen and Y, so Y (the end) is eligible; U, Z, Q and R are backs
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 0.9, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 0.9, -1.0, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 0.9, 1.0, "T"),
       D("RE", "DE", 0.9, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.0, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.0, 1.2, "M"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 2.6, 7.6, "S"), D("NB", "NB", 2.6, -8.4, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -13.0, "CB"),
       D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 12.5, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=107, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: a direct snap at the 3")
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-8.5, 13.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.4, -11.5), (-1.5, -8.0), "the quarterback,\nsplit out")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-6.4, 6.4), (-5.0, 0.0), "direct snap\nto the back")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The default is a run by the back who takes the snap, behind the wing tight end as an extra blocker; the trick is
a pass by that back; and the men not to forget are the tight ends.** This is the direct-snap look from the trick-play
section. The back can run without a handoff, which gives the offense an extra blocker in the count, and the
quarterback, standing in the slot as a receiver, takes a defender with him. The defense's eyes go to the back and
to the quarterback (everyone knows the quarterback can catch out there). What it tends to forget is that the back
can throw, and that the tight ends, the players who block on almost every goal-line snap, are eligible: Y is the
end of the line and U is a back on the wing. In Week 5 of 2025 at Cincinnati, Detroit took a direct snap to David
Montgomery on second-and-3 from the 3, and Montgomery threw a touchdown pass to tight end Brock Wright.[^cin] If the
defense covers the quarterback and the back's run, a tight end is the most likely target.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Detroit's 2021 rebuild had two halves: build the lines and the core through the draft (Sewell, Hutchinson, St.
  Brown, Gibbs, LaPorta), and **choose variance** as an underdog. The fourth-down aggression came before the good team
  did.
- **Ben Johnson's offense (2022–2024)** was a familiar run and play-action base with four habits on top: the
  quarterback **under center** (the league's highest share in 2022 and 2024), **heavy and jumbo personnel with a
  reported lineman**, **shifts layered with motion**, and **trick plays built as constraint plays**. Each makes
  one snap look like several; each costs drilling time, play clock and the occasional disaster.
- **Campbell's fourth downs** led the league in neutral go rate in 2022–2024 and, by a rough yardstick, gained about
  `{python} S["det_gain"]` points over kicking in five seasons, most of it in 2024. The extra, longer attempts were
  worth far less than the short ones: aggression has diminishing returns.
- Defenses used the standard counters (a boot-side end who stays home, an owner for the reported lineman, more
  single-high, simpler motion rules), and the offense still ranked near the top every year. What finally broke it
  up was the coaching market: other teams **hired its coordinators**. Johnson went to the Bears and
  Glenn to the Jets in January 2025. Detroit then went through Morton, Campbell calling plays and, in 2026, Petzing:
  three coordinators in three years.
- **What transferred:** in one season Chicago's under-center, play-action and trick-play rates jumped to near the top
  of the league and Detroit's fell back; motion and reported linemen moved less. The **play-caller's signature
  habits moved with him**, the **fourth-down habit stayed with the head coach**, and the Bears' results moved with
  help from a rebuilt line and a second-year quarterback.
